Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
Recently, the rulings on timing for additional strike declaration and
damage prevention were reversed. Playing those kinds of cards was
brought into line with the general priority-passing scheme used in most
aspects of the game.

The controversy around the blocking and deflection timing has me
thinking it might be valuable to apply the same principles, and remedy,
to the rules surrounding playing reaction cards and blocking.

The rules, as outlines in 6.2.2 don't restrict what kinds of reaction
cards can be played except to say intercept can only be played when it
is needed. This implies other kinds of reactions can be played, even
during a block attempt.

I would suggest a successful block occurs when:

1. A block attempt has been announced.
2. Intercept of the blocking minion is >= stealth of the acting minion
3. Priority, and the option play effects, has passed around as per
1.6.1.5. and everyone has passed

Is that just a restatement of the current rules? Would adopting that
definition bring blocking and reacting more into line with other
aspects of the game? Would it eliminate the need for some of the
current reaction rulings?

An acting player saying "you block" would translate to "I
pass". The reacting player would still get the opportunity to pay
effects (handing priority back the actor) - wake a different minion,
play deflection, etc... They couldn't announce a different block
attempt.

Traffic on the other thread suggests many players don't feel the
ruling on deflection timing is well-grounded in the rules. There does
not seem to be a similar objection to the ruling that you can't play
Deflection after you announce a block attempt (until it fails). But the
two rulings do seem equally well (or un) justified.

Should we do away with both?

-Ben Swainbank

Messages.Author: Kushiel
Messages.Body:
Ben Swainbank wrote:
> An acting player saying "you block" would translate to "I
> pass". The reacting player would still get the opportunity to pay
> effects (handing priority back the actor) - wake a different minion,
> play deflection, etc... They couldn't announce a different block

I'm pretty sure they can only play reaction cards that won't do
anything to mess with the current block attempt. You can Wake a second
minion, because that doesn't affect the current block attempt. Ditto
reducing a bleed. Bouncing a bleed DOES affect the current block
attempt, though, which is why I think it's forbidden.

> Traffic on the other thread suggests many players don't feel the
> ruling on deflection timing is well-grounded in the rules. There does
> not seem to be a similar objection to the ruling that you can't play
> Deflection after you announce a block attempt (until it fails).

I think that's just because it hasn't really come up at all in that
other thread. Could be that it did and I missed it, though.

> But the
> two rulings do seem equally well (or un) justified.

They don't to me.

> Should we do away with both?

Nope. Deflecting during a successful block is an counterintuitive to me
as is cancelling a Deflection equalling the deflectors stating that
they don't block (if they never stated it).

John Eno

I did a fair bit of groping for answers in my initial post. It's coming
together for me now.

I am concerned with key aspects of the game where the rules exist in
the form of rulings rather than the rule book or card text. I am less
concerned about whether players can play deflection before announcing
block attempts.

I advocate the following (which may be what LSJ is doing (has done) and
may be restatements of the existing rules):

If there are restrictions about when bleed redirection cards can be
played (and players seem to agree that there should be some) then those
restrictions should be added as card text. That text could be "not
playable during a block attempt or after a successful block" it could
be "only usable after blocks are declined".

The existing rulings about Deflection timing should be voided
(reversed, moot, etc...). A reaction card could be printed that
redirected a bleed with different (or no) timing restrictions.

After an acting player says "you block" priority passes. A reacting
player has the opportunity to play more effects. For example, if a
reaction card reduced intercept, it could be played at this time, and
potentially result in a non-block (following more priority passing).
Presumably, this is not new, but I expect it's sufficiently non-clear
that I won't embarrass myself by pointing it out.

-Ben Swainbank

Messages.Author: Bram Vink
Messages.Body:
LSJ schreef:



It seems to me that the ruling "cannot interrupt a block attempt with
cards that change the target of the action (ie. can't play deflection
while blocking)" is the one currently used by most people.

Also, the ruling on deflection et al. only being playable after
blocking (ie. playing deflection means you do not block) seems to me,
and if I'm not mistaken from the thread, counterintuitive to most
people.

Given that almost all options, apart from cornercase card cancellation
in the case of not waiting to play the deflection in case action
modifiers after declaring not to block, are covered by the first
ruling, and that the second ruling apparently is new to people, I would
suggest sticking to the first ruling (ie. can't play deflection while
blocking) if only for the sake of popular vote on intuitive play.

Over here we've always played that tossing in pool means you're not
blocking, btw. ;)

B
